title: Why You Shouldn't “Build Community”
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin distinguishes organic community from the manufactured version common in schools — circle activities, kind letters, and morning meetings designed to force camaraderie — arguing the manufactured version fails on five counts: it's fake because forced sentiment produces cognitive dissonance students silently resist; it's meaningless because compliments given under compulsion carry no weight and embarrass the recipient; it's dishonest because activities that aren't real amount to a lie; it's awkward because being put on the spot discomforts many students; and it wastes time better spent on academics. His alternative is three genuine mechanisms: protecting students from bullying and disruption so they feel safe enough to open up, ensuring that safety through expert, consistent classroom management, and using competition — recess games, academic contests, debates — which he says builds real camaraderie far better than any manufactured activity. He frames the teacher's job as empowering and equipping students academically, not managing their feelings or beliefs.
points: Manufactured community-building (circles, kind letters, morning meetings) is fake and produces cognitive dissonance students silently resist.
Forced compliments are meaningless and often embarrass the recipient, who knows the sentiment was compelled.
Genuine community comes from protecting students from bullying and disruption so they feel safe enough to open up.
Expert, consistent classroom management is what actually guarantees that safety, more than any planned activity.
Competition — recess games, academic contests, debates — builds real camaraderie far better than manufactured exercises.
quotes: In educational parlance, building community means to manufacture it.
You can’t force community. You can only set up conditions that nurture it. Otherwise, students will resist.
Tell a student they must say or write something nice about someone and they’ll do it, but if it’s not from the heart and of their own volition, then it’s hot air.
By far the most important and effective way to build community is to protect your students from bullying, name-calling, and disruption.
Competition builds new friendships, camaraderie, and community quickly and far better than a thousand kind letters.
So much is wasted on fluff and nonsense that take away from the one thing that helps students and their future more than anything else: Academics.
